# Le Tsuan Design — Full Project Case Studies

> This file expands on llms.txt with the complete technical write-up for every project in the portfolio: client, location, year, category, and the full case-study narrative including design methodology, engineering details, and material specifications. Sourced directly from each project's live page.


---

## R.O.C. Air Force Academy 90th Founding Anniversary

*Corridor of Light: A Special Exhibition on Academy History*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-air-force-academy.dc.html


**CLIENT:** R.O.C. Air Force Academy · **LOCATION:** Kaohsiung, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2019 · **AREA:** 396.6948 ㎡ · **CATEGORY:** Curation, Exhibition Design, Graphic Design, Visual Design, Interactive Multimedia, Construction


#### A Timeline You Walk Through
The exhibition's circulation follows the Academy's own chronology, and every stop marks another step forward, moving from the Academy's past into its present.
#### Prologue: Dreaming of the Sky
Walk in, and the first thing you meet is a feature wall with real presence, aviation-inspired geometric lines that plant the idea of "Air Force" in your mind before you've even moved further in.
#### Founding and Wartime Years
Old photographs, documents, and artifacts are laid out plainly, without dressing anything up. The resilience of those cadets, in those hard years, speaks for itself.
#### Modernization and a New Generation of Airpower
From fighter jet models to the evolution of equipment, you can trace how the Air Force grew from its rough early days into the force it is today.
#### Looking Forward: Education and Legacy
This zone ties the Academy's mission of training talent to the future of aerospace, so the exhibition looks ahead as much as it looks back.
#### The History Timeline Wall
This wall is the backbone of the whole exhibition's storytelling. Every major event across the Air Force's ninety years is marked on the wall in chronological order, with a single line running through it all, tying scattered moments into one continuous story. From the founding, through the war, through the relocation and rebuilding, every point in time sits on that line. Walking along it, you end up somewhere past reading a record: closer to walking through ninety years.
#### Wing Forms and Light
The ceiling takes on the streamlined shape of an aircraft wing, lit to evoke clouds against an open sky. The space itself says "Air Force" without needing a single word of text.
#### Display Cases and Artifact Presentation
The cases use high transparency, anti-reflective glass with carefully controlled lighting, so medals, artifacts, and uniforms are seen at their best, while still meeting the standards artifact preservation demands.
#### Models and Immersive Scenes
At the center of the exhibition sit aircraft models and recreated scenes rather than flat panels on a wall, giving visitors a much stronger sense of presence, much closer to being there.
#### Closing
The exhibition lays out historical material, but its real work is bringing the weight of military heritage together with the language of modern exhibition design. Anyone who walks through should be able to feel it, that drive, carried down from ninety years ago, that's still unmistakably Air Force.

## Amazing Homeland

*Cheng-Hsiung Chen’s Collection of Taiwanese Indigenous Artifacts*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-amazing-homeland.dc.html


**CLIENT:** National Museum of History · **LOCATION:** Taipei, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2017 · **CATEGORY:** Exhibition Design, Graphic Design, Visual Design, Construction


#### A Low-Light Room, Built Around the Objects
The exhibition sits inside a deliberately low-illuminance museum atmosphere. Lighting is controlled with enough precision that visual noise disappears and each artifact emerges on its own, inside its own pool of light. Nothing decorative competes for attention; the eye stays on the craftsmanship.
#### 01 Garment Gallery, A Suspended Theater of Light
Long garments hang from a suspended tension system, each piece held by fine steel cables in front of a clean, off-white main wall, which gives the fabric a sense of lightness and floating. Every garment gets its own anti-glare spotlight, angled precisely to bring out the three-dimensional luster of glass beads, embroidery appliqués, and fur textures. Information plaques stay low on the wall and minimal, so they never compete with the pieces themselves.
#### 02 Terminus Feature, The Aesthetics of Woven Identity
The circulation ends at a monumental, full-height traditional woven tapestry that closes out the route. An interlaced diamond pattern in red, black, and blue-green covers the entire surface, forming the strongest visual punctuation point of the whole journey and standing in as a contemporary answer to the exhibition's core idea: that woven pattern is identity worn on the body.
#### 03 Basketry and Pottery Gallery, An Immersive Corridor of Living
From here the space shifts into a dark, immersive corridor. A mist-black floor and deep purple-grey walls pair with white graphic panels in a low-contrast palette that lets the artifacts' own natural colors carry the room.
On one side, OSB shelving holds daily objects like baskets and wooden mortars, lit from below by warm 3000K linear strips recessed under each shelf, the light washing upward to outline the objects and add a lived-in warmth against the otherwise solemn tone.
On the other side, glass vitrines and freestanding plinths hold pottery jars and urns, each one spotlighted on a black pedestal like an actor under a stage light. Black retractable stanchions choreograph the flow through this section, balancing protection for the artifacts against the pace of viewing.
#### 04 Sculpture and Fine Pottery Gallery, A Sanctuary of Time
The final gallery is built as a quiet sanctuary. A continuous run of full-height glass vitrines sits against a dark, reflective floor, and the reflections stretch the space into a deep, serene depth. Stone carvings, ceramic figures, and pots each get their own micro-spotlight and a suspended caption panel, and visitors move through it the way they might move through a corridor of time, the contrast between low ambient light and sharp accent lighting giving weight to the history each piece carries.
#### Design Language
Lighting strategy: low ambient illuminance paired with high-precision accent lighting. Material palette: blackened steel plinths, dark wood flooring, off-white walls, OSB shelving. The whole exhibition runs on one consistent museum logic, dark environment, bright artifact, softened by warm light details built into the shelving, holding a careful balance between solemnity and warmth so that attention keeps returning to the object itself.

## See the Ministry of Culture

*One History. Six Departments. Countless Everyday Moments.*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-art-gallery-culture.dc.html


**CLIENT:** Ministry of Culture · **YEAR:** 2019 · **CATEGORY:** Curation, Exhibition Design, Graphic Design, Interactive Multimedia, Construction


#### Curatorial Concept: A Package Waiting to Be Opened
A sealed box gives away nothing about what it holds until someone unwraps it, lays it flat, and lets it spread open panel by panel into what packaging designers call a die-line.
The history of the Ministry of Culture works the same way. It runs from the founding of the Council for Cultural Affairs in the 1980s, through the Government Information Office's role in media and communications, to the Ministry's own establishment in 2012, and each of those organizational restructurings reads like a fold line pressed into the packaging.
What the Ministry does today, across its various bureaus and divisions, is the content that only becomes visible once the box is unfolded. The exhibition takes "Unfold, See the Ministry of Culture" as its curatorial theme, using the packaging die-line as both visual language and spatial framework: visitors move through the space the way they'd unwrap a gift by hand, watching each fold line of the Ministry's history flatten out and become legible until they arrive at a clear picture of what the Ministry actually does.
#### The Unfolding Diagram as Narrative Structure
In packaging design, the unfolding diagram is the flat pattern a three-dimensional box produces when it's opened out. Its panels, the lid, the side flaps, the base, the corner tabs, are connected but distinct: folded, they form a complete box; flattened, they read like separate pages.
That structural logic became the exhibition's narrative framework on two levels at once. Each fold line in the diagram lines up with a milestone in the Ministry's history (the founding of the Council for Cultural Affairs, the absorption of the Government Information Office's functions, the Ministry's inauguration), so crossing a fold line means completing a chapter of the story. Each panel, meanwhile, lines up with one of the Ministry's current bureaus or affiliated agencies, so visitors leave understanding both where the Ministry came from and what it oversees now, without needing two separate systems to explain it.
#### Circulation: From Sealed Box to Unfolded Diagram
The circulation follows the psychological experience of unwrapping a package, in three stages. The entrance is a monumental sealed packing box showing only the Ministry's emblem and minimal text, building curiosity before the unwrapping even starts.
Past the entrance, the space opens into an actual unfolding-diagram floor and wall layout, so visitors feel like they're walking across a flattened box. Each fold line they cross carries them into the next historical period; each panel functions as its own zone introducing one division. Mapped against the Ministry's current structure: the lid panel belongs to the Department of Planning, which sets cultural policy direction, mid- and long-term plans, and cross-sector coordination, and sits at the "lid" as the overview entry point before the six functional panels.
The six side-flap panels cover the Ministry's six operational bureaus: the Department of Cultural Resources (heritage, museums, community development, cultural facilities), the Department of Cultural Industries (creative-industry development, cross-strait economic exchange, technology), the Department of Motion Pictures and Popular Music Industries (film, radio, television, popular music policy), the Department of Humanities and Publications (literary development, publishing, government publications), the Department of Arts (visual arts, performing arts, everyday aesthetics), and the Department of Cultural Exchange (international and cross-strait cultural cooperation).
The base panel closes with a summary timeline of the Ministry's history, looping back up to the Department of Planning at the lid, so the spatial logic runs from historical context to policy direction and back again. At the exit, echoing the sealed box at the entrance, an interactive installation invites visitors to "re-seal" the package by choosing the Ministry function that matters most to them and marking it on a digital box surface, leaving behind their own hope for what comes next.
#### Visual and Graphic Design
The visual identity system runs on fold lines, cut lines, and registration marks (the crosshair symbols used in print production), appearing consistently across the wayfinding system, panel borders, and timeline nodes.
The color scheme builds on the Ministry's brand colors, with each panel assigned its own secondary accent by content theme, much like color blocks separate product lines in packaging design, so visitors know at a glance which division they're standing in.
Each panel is kept to what can be read at a glance, so the diagram's clean visual character isn't buried under dense text; anything deeper is handed off to the interactive touch points.
#### Exhibit and Interactive Design
Floor and wall lighting shifts as visitors cross each fold line, reinforcing the sense of time advancing and structure unfolding. The departmental multimedia stations are the core of the interactive design, built to answer one specific need: letting the public see what each department actually does and where national cultural policy currently stands.
Each of the six functional panels carries a touchscreen station with three layers of content. The first layer is an at-a-glance infographic of the department's core responsibilities. The second layer tracks what's happening now: current flagship policies and project status (the Department of Cultural Resources' heritage restoration work, the Department of Cultural Industries' support programs, the Department of Motion Pictures and Popular Music Industries' grants and incentives, and so on), supplied by each department and refreshed on a regular cycle so the content stays current. The third layer points forward, linking to the Ministry's official website or open-data resources so visitors who want to can keep following policy after they leave.
All six stations share one interface language, layout, department color coding, and iconography, so visitors can identify what they're looking at even browsing out of order. The lid-panel station for the Department of Planning uses dynamic data visualization to show how the six departments' work coordinates, giving visitors an overview before they go deeper, and doubles as the navigational index for the six panels.
At the exit, the interactive re-sealing wall collects visitors' hopes and feedback on cultural policy, closing the narrative loop back to the sealed box at the entrance while giving the Ministry a channel for public input.
#### Structure, Materials, and Lighting
The building's occupancy permit calculated the entire ground floor as a single area, which meant anything fixed to the structure would trigger a formal interior-alteration review. To leave that permit status untouched, the whole exhibition was designed as non-fixed construction: every plinth, panel, and volume stands free, anchored to neither the slab nor the beams and columns.
The trade-off was that center of gravity, ballasting, and overturning risk had to be verified element by element to keep the gallery safe under crowd loading and seismic activity, and this ended up being the most time-consuming technical problem on the project.
The primary structure uses clean white and light-gray volumes, in keeping with the durable, no-nonsense character expected of a government exhibition space, while select panels bring in corrugated-cardboard texture or matte finishes as a material echo of packaging, kept just short of tipping into a commercial look. The main circulation runs on even ambient lighting; fold lines and panel edges are traced with linear light strips to reinforce the diagram's structural lines; and key installations, like the emblem-reveal device, get focused spot lighting for a sense of ceremony.
#### Closing
The unfolding diagram isn't a visual gimmick so much as a narrative tool matched to what this exhibition needed to do: turning organizational history, the kind of material that usually ends up as a bullet list or an official document, into something visitors unwrap by hand and understand step by step. What visitors carry out isn't only the history from the Council for Cultural Affairs to the present Ministry, but a sense that what the Ministry actually does sits closer to daily life than they expected.

## The Lawn Needed More Protection Than the Artwork Did

*2013 Asian Art Biennial*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-asian-art-biennial.dc.html


**CLIENT:** National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts · **LOCATION:** Taichung, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2013-2014 · **CATEGORY:** Construction


#### Ten Light Boxes, One Lawn That Couldn't Be Damaged
In 2013, the artist collective LuxuryLogico took part in the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts' "2013 Asian Art Biennial: Everyday Life" with a piece called I LOVE TAIWAN, using a large array of light-box installations to turn a well-worn Taiwanese catchphrase into a variable-scale outdoor artwork scattered across the museum's lawn. We handled the on-site construction and fabrication of the piece.
#### The Lawn Was Part of the Work
The site was the museum's expansive outdoor lawn, which functioned as both backdrop and part of the artwork's effect: light boxes standing scattered across the green, lighting up at night into a landscape of light. There was one non-negotiable requirement for the build: fix and wire all ten light boxes without damaging the lawn itself. That ruled out the heavy machinery normally used for outdoor construction, large-scale foundation excavation, and anything that would leave exposed soil or compaction marks behind, since the lawn's condition was tied directly to how the artwork looked and to the museum's ongoing maintenance obligations.
#### Building Without a Trace
For each light box's post and base, we skipped pouring concrete altogether and designed a custom base component to carry the load instead, using a low-disturbance fixing method that avoided large-scale digging. Power cabling between the ten light boxes ran along existing hard-paved surfaces wherever possible, or was buried shallow underground, cutting down how often equipment had to be dragged across the grass.
We used manual labor and small tools instead of heavy machinery, working zone by zone in batches so the foot traffic and load on any one section of lawn stayed within what it could recover from. Large canvas sheets covered the main routes and work areas, so all foot traffic, tool storage, and material handling sat on canvas rather than directly on the grass.
Once each installation was positioned, we checked the lawn zone by zone, backfilling and leveling any compression marks or loosened soil so the surface was flat again before opening day. With teardown in mind, the light-box structures and materials were chosen for roughly 90% recyclability, so most of the material could be reused or recycled once the show closed rather than becoming waste.
#### Result
The ten-light-box I LOVE TAIWAN installation went up across the museum's outdoor lawn without incident, hidden among the greenery by day and lighting up into a sea of text by night. The lawn came through the install exactly as it went in.

## Beyond Just an Exhibition–You Are Part of the Art!

*Step Into a Breathing Magical Universe of Light and Shadows*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-beyond-just-an-exhibition.dc.html


**CLIENT:** teamLab · **LOCATION:** Taipei, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2024 · **AREA:** 1,785.126㎡ · **CATEGORY:** Exhibition Design, Installation Art, Event


#### It Wasn't the Wall Moving, It Was the Wind
Seventh floor, south wing special exhibition zone, National Taiwan Science Education Center. A quiet floor was turned, in fourteen days, into a breathing forest: creatures in the Bouncing Valley wake beside your footsteps, spheres of light echo a rolling soundtrack, fruit on the slide scatters with the sound of children's laughter. teamLab Future Park Taipei unfolded here, and out of sight of every visitor, an entire floor's slabs, trusses, power, and light had all been recalculated, over and over.
This is a 1,785.126 square meter site, fitted out with 178 projectors, plus backend blending processors, wireless access points, and computer terminals, together weaving a sensing network that reacts to visitor behavior in real time. We handled the spatial planning, produced the construction drawings, and served as the general contractor for every on-site requirement, from day one of mobilization to teardown and clearance within seven days of closing, present through the entire run.
#### Hanging a Playground From a Floor You Can't Drill Into
This system demanded extreme precision. A large array of projectors had to be edge-blended with virtually no tolerance for misalignment, made harder by equipment that was already older and well used. Getting an international-standard blend out of aging hardware was, on its own, a delicate balancing act, and before any of that software could run, an entire invisible skeleton had to hold it up.
Projectors, speakers, and sensors hang from a truss below the 8th-floor slab, and the combined weight of 178 devices was never something to estimate by eye. We used custom threaded rods and steel plates to calculate and distribute the load of every device across the truss structure. Once complete, every node held steady, with no sagging or loosening anywhere in the array.
The raised access flooring underfoot carried its own challenge: in places it ran as high as 2.5 meters off the slab. At that height and span, we reinforced the structure with tightly spaced supports and additional steel, while routing the cabling through the void beneath, so load-bearing capacity and cable maintenance could coexist.
The wall was another problem. Most of the venue's walls run six meters high, and this is a public venue where none of them could be drilled or fastened into. We used a structural tie-in method instead, lashing the partitions and support structures to the existing structure behind them. When the work was inspected, the wall surfaces were untouched, exactly as they'd been before.
Curved floor-to-ceiling glass ran along two sides of the venue, and the exits, entrance, and gift shop all sat next to bright or open spaces. Interactive projection is extremely sensitive to ambient light, and any leak of outside light or reflection could throw off the projected image and confuse the sensing system.
We worked through the two curved glass walls and every entrance, exit, and shop-adjacent route one at a time, blocking light while preserving both visitor flow and fire-exit requirements, until the entire floor held as a proper blackout space.
With 178 projectors plus blending processors, access points, and terminals all running at once, power demand went far beyond what a typical exhibition space draws, so we reconfigured the electrical system from scratch. Part of the circuit runs on Hypalon cable, chosen for its resistance to abrasion, weather, and heat, and its flexibility, built to survive being routed again and again through the truss and under the raised floor as conditions shifted. Fourteen days, and all of it had to come together at once.
#### The Wall Never Moved
The real challenge only began after opening. The higher a system's blending precision, the less interference it can tolerate, and partway through the run, the projected image began drifting out of alignment. The initial suspicion on site fell on the wall itself. We didn't rush to a conclusion. We mounted displacement sensors on the wall, marked reference points, and had someone log readings on site every day. The data built up day by day, and the answer became clear: the wall hadn't moved.
If it wasn't the wall, the problem had to be in the projectors themselves. We added gyroscopic sensors, transmitting readings daily to track the projectors' own micro-vibration over time, narrowing in zone by zone on where the drift kept showing up. The pieces came together: the problem clustered around the summer months, during the busiest visitor periods.
The cause turned out to be almost absurdly simple. Staff, trying to keep visitors comfortable, had turned the air conditioning up to maximum. The vents had already been positioned away from the projector housings, but the stronger airflow was still enough to cause a barely perceptible vibration in the units, and that was enough to throw the blended image out of alignment.
We didn't turn the airflow down, since that would have meant trading visitor comfort for image stability. The real fix was re-wrapping and tightening the ductwork, redirecting the airflow path away from the area around each projector. Airflow stayed exactly as it was, the projectors stopped shaking, and the drift problem was resolved. What maintenance remained through the rest of the run was a separate matter, wear and tear from visitors interacting with the installations, requiring periodic servicing.
Another thread of the investigation was just as stubborn: HDMI chips began burning out in several zones. Tracing it back, we found the signal cable and power cable had all been bundled together on site, and some runs used extra-long HDMI cable to carry the signal directly over distance instead of going through a proper signal extender. The static that built up gradually damaged the chips inside the HDMI cabling.
On top of that, the computer terminals had simply been set on wire shelving with no insulation at all, adding to the static buildup. We added insulating mats under the equipment, and this kind of chip failure dropped off noticeably from there.
#### What the Drawings Didn't Show
Not every problem shows up on a drawing. Partway through the run, visitors began reporting a jarring impact at the bottom of the Fruit Field slide, and one visitor even produced a medical note. We assessed the situation and traced the cause to the original slide's angle, not something we could look past. We worked with the client's technical team to propose a corrected slide angle, carried out the on-site retrofit on a closed day, and adjusted the angle to soften the landing. We never heard another report of the issue afterward.
None of this troubleshooting happened behind closed doors. The suspicion about wall displacement was something our own team stayed on, reading the sensor data day after day, point by point, until it resolved. Every adjustment to floor load and power capacity had to be checked first against the venue's structural limits with the facilities team. Blocking light at the glass walls touched the fire-exit routes, which meant bringing in the fire department to sign off before we could seal anything for good.
#### Seven Days to Zero
When the exhibition closed, all 178 projectors, the blending processors, the access points, the computer terminals, the sensor units, the entire truss-suspension system, the raised-floor structural reinforcement, and every partition wall had to be fully dismantled and cleared within seven days, returning the site to exactly the condition it was handed over in, ready for the venue's next scheduled exhibition.

## Cat Art Museum

*A Super-Healing World by Shu Yamamoto*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-cat-art.dc.html


**CLIENT:** Cat Art Museum · **LOCATION:** Pingtung, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2024 · **CATEGORY:** Exhibition Design, Graphic Design, Visual Design, Installation Art, Construction


#### Stepping Into a Painting
Walk into "CATART," Japanese artist Shu Yamamoto's cat-themed exhibition in Pingtung, and the paintings on the wall stop staying flat. We handled the overall spatial planning, color strategy, and the work of turning two-dimensional paintings into three-dimensional installations and immersive scenes for the show.
#### The Challenge
The collection spans both Eastern and Western art traditions and jumps across visual styles, so the core design question was how to give each group of works its own fitting stage through spatial language, and then link those stages into one visitor journey with a clear rhythm and something memorable at every turn.
#### Color as the Backbone
Instead of the neutral white-box gallery convention, we split the space into large, saturated color zones, olive green, caramel yellow, lavender, magenta, indigo, arranged in sequence so visitors feel the emotional shift as they move through, without needing to read a single wall text. Arched signage panels at each corner fold the curatorial text directly into the architecture, so there's no separate placard breaking up the walls.
#### Bringing the Paintings Off the Wall
Select characters from the paintings were reproduced at true scale as large-format figures and sculptures, paired with dedicated lighting and background murals, letting them step out of their frames. For scenes tied to a specific setting, we extended the mural into real furniture, matching hand-painted backdrops and physical props precisely in perspective, light, and shadow so visitors could sit directly into the scene. This translation work was the most technically demanding part of the project, requiring tight coordination between mural painting, custom prop fabrication, and spatial scale.
Each stylistically distinct series also got its own material and formal vocabulary, from geometric 3D display walls, to a backlit installation referencing cathedral stained glass, to a pop-art line-drawing wall and a fountain-based set piece, so every zone carries its own identity instead of repeating one display formula.
The entire second floor was planned around a dimensional photo zone concept: every corner and leftover pocket of space was designed in advance as its own photo point, turning the circulation path into a continuous, uninterrupted experience rather than a plain passageway.
#### Light and Flow
Track-mounted spotlighting runs throughout, with angle and color temperature adjusted individually for each artwork and installation, keeping the overall space low-lit while the content pops off the walls. The route is segmented by wall corners, so visitors keep running into a sense of discovery as they move through.
#### What Visitors Actually Do There
Every zone has become a natural hotspot for visitor photos since opening, and social media reach has followed. The design set out to let visitors, once inside, do more than look at paintings: they get pulled gently into the process of becoming a cat themselves: walking into the paintings, exploring the giant stained-glass window of "Cat Light," visiting the cats-only "Cat Palace," and wandering through scenes exclusive to Pingtung: cats napping on Dawan Island, a cat fountain, a kitten's birth, a cat café, a starlit cat night. Each zone reinterprets the world through a cat's eyes, languid, playful, unbound, and no art-historical knowledge is needed to enjoy any of it.


---

## Points of Light in Grayscale: Turning an Odd-Shaped Plot into a Destination

*Ørsted Pavilion, 2023 Changhua Flower Festival*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-changhua-flower.dc.html


**CLIENT:** Ørsted / Changhua County Government · **LOCATION:** Changhua, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2023 · **CATEGORY:** Graphic Design, Construction, Garden Design


#### A Leftover Corner, and What Grew There
Ørsted took part in the 2023 Changhua International Flower Festival with a corporate pavilion built around the theme "Green Wind, Sustainable Changhua." The site assigned to it sat in an awkward, constrained corner of the park, where existing concrete steps and concrete piers were already fixed in place, boxing in both circulation and display layout before design work even started.
#### Building on What Was Already There
Rather than working around those structures, we redefined the concrete piers as the fixed base for the main feature wall. That single decision solved two problems together: it gave the outdoor display a ready-made concrete foundation against the structural risks of long-term wind, rain, and weather exposure, and it folded a constraint that had originally felt unwanted into the landscape narrative itself, so structural performance and spatial aesthetics answered to the same move.
#### Color Against a Grey Season
The planting plan had its own problem: the exhibition period landed in the off-season for winter blooms, so the range of available flower material was limited. We compared options and settled on shrub species in auspicious, festive colors instead of the usual seasonal flowers, and, given the low ambient brightness typical of overcast winter weather, deliberately went with a high-saturation, high-brightness palette.
Against the grayscale backdrop of the season, the pavilion stood out sharply, and more or less by accident became the brightest spot in the park. The planted wall was paired with a backdrop depicting Ørsted's Greater Changhua offshore wind farm, giving the company's sustainability message a form visitors could see and feel directly.
#### Result
This constrained, awkward corner ended up as the most popular photo spot in the park during the Lunar New Year period. The structural limitations weren't worked around; they got built directly into the wall.


---

## Detective Conan

*Science Investigation Exhibition – Taipei & Kaohsiung*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-detective-conan-taipei.dc.html


**LOCATION:** National Taiwan Science Education Center, TaipeiNational Science and Technology Museum, Kaohsiung · **YEAR:** 2019–2020 · **CATEGORY:** Exhibition Design, Interior Design, Graphic Design, Visual Design, Construction


#### Turning a Detective Story Into a Crowd-Flow Plan
The exhibition adapts a mystery in which a novel starring Kogoro Mouri is about to be published, only for its author to turn up dead at home with "14:00 Kogoro Mouri" written in his appointment book, making Mouri the prime suspect overnight. Visitors don't watch this story from the outside; they step into the crime scene and use forensic science to clear Mouri's name and find the real killer. We were responsible for turning this Japanese licensed IP exhibition into a physical build that worked within Taiwanese venue conditions, covering circulation planning, set reconstruction, interactive-device integration, and post-show teardown, across two venues in Taipei and Kaohsiung.
#### One Script, Two Buildings
The exhibition runs two staggered circulation tracks, a hardcore forensics route following Conan and Amuro, and a lighter deduction route following Conan and Ran, which naturally splits the crowd inside the venue. A three-stage narrative circulation, crime scene investigation, clue exploration, science lab, uses wall transitions and pacing to make visitors feel the case advancing as they move through the space.
Wall structures for the crime scene, the Mouri Detective Agency, and the Poirot Cafe were all cross-checked against footage and panels from the original anime and manga beforehand, matching scene proportions, furniture placement, signage typography, and color tone so the physical rooms held up against what visitors remembered from the screen.
Because Taipei and Kaohsiung differ in scale, we redesigned the wall templates and scene-transition circulation for each venue while keeping the same level of research fidelity, so the same IP scenes could deliver a consistent experience in two different buildings.
#### Queuing Had to Be Designed Too
The biggest risk to an immersive exhibition usually isn't weak content, it's crowds locking up at a single point. We mapped the known bottlenecks ahead of time: the ticketing counter and QR-code redemption point at the entrance, the audio-guide rental counter, the first crime-scene set (a high-density photo spot right at entry), the forensic devices in the science lab zone, the manuscript gallery, and the gift shop near the exit. Any one of these could form a long queue during peak hours.
The manuscript gallery bans photography and sees low interaction but long dwell times, so we placed it near the end of the route and widened its corridor to keep it from backing up the flow behind it. For the other hotspots, we used different weekday and weekend opening hours to spread crowds across time. The dual-route booklet system itself worked as a natural flow-splitter, with entrance guidance adjusted dynamically according to real-time crowd data on each route. The forensic-device zones used multi-station parallel setups, with two or more workstations each for fingerprint and handwriting analysis, cutting down dwell time at any single point.
Corridor widths at key scene nodes were calculated directly, working backward from maximum simultaneous occupancy multiplied by average dwell time in seconds, with buffer zones placed behind major photo spots so photo-taking wouldn't back up the flow behind it. A physical partition and separate checkout line ran between the gift shop and the paid exhibition zone, so free-entry foot traffic and paying visitors were counted separately, reducing the impact of end-of-route congestion on overall evacuation.
During summer peak season, electronic displays at the ticketing area showed real-time wait estimates, and additional staff enforced capacity control at each zone's entrance, so exhibition quality and safe evacuation held at the same time.
#### Four Forensic Devices
Voiceprint analysis, handwriting analysis, fingerprint analysis, and blood analysis each run as an independent interactive device, chained together into one complete line of evidence, so solving the mystery is a layered accumulation of deduction rather than a single guess.
The detective's notebook works as the core puzzle tool rather than a souvenir, guiding visitors to record clues on site, cross-reference witness statements, and verify their conclusions in the science lab zone, turning wall-panel reading into active evidence-gathering. The mystery resolves on a single sheet of paper revealing the truth of the case, and the closing zone uses reinforced lighting and sound to make that reveal the emotional high point of the experience.
#### After Closing
Once the exhibition ended, we tore down the set walls, props, and electrical wiring and returned the site to venue management. After the Taipei teardown, some reusable components were packaged, transported, and refurbished for direct use at the Kaohsiung venue, so the same precisely calculated exhibition logic didn't need to be recalculated from zero for the second city.


---

## Detention

*Reality Experience*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-detention-pier2.dc.html


**LOCATION:** Songshan Cultural and Creative Park, TaipeiThe Pier2 Art Center, Kaohsiung · **YEAR:** 2020–2021 · **AREA:** Songshan: 1,210 ㎡Pier2: 1,190.2 ㎡ · **CATEGORY:** Exhibition Design, Interior Design, Graphic Design, Visual Design, Construction


#### Horror-Movie Logic Meets Fire-Code Logic
The exhibition adapts Detention, the suspense-horror PC game Red Candle Games released in 2017 to widespread acclaim, marking the team's first attempt at turning a single-player game into a multi-layered immersive experience. A 991.737㎡ version of Cuihua High School was rebuilt from the ground up at Songshan Cultural and Creative Park, with a classroom zone, restroom zone, principal's office, music room, counseling room, infirmary, and the "Endless Corridor." Visitors take on the role of a reading-club member, stepping into the loop the game's protagonist, Fang Ray-shin, experiences.
#### Sixty Years of Wear, Built From Scratch
We collected genuine 1960s Taiwanese school-campus objects on the ground: a classic Tatung fan, a black rotary-dial telephone, an old dial radio, wooden double desks and chairs, a hand-crank alarm siren, propaganda-era slogan frames, and old-style censer altars. Anything we couldn't source was custom-fabricated based on historical research and finished with professional aging techniques, until material, color, and wear patterns were indistinguishable from real period artifacts.
Even the chalk handwriting on the blackboard, the typeface of warning slogans like "Report Communist Spies," and the formatting of official documents were researched to match the era exactly.
Walls were coated in cement paint using a slapping technique, a splatter technique, and high-pressure air-drying, layering up peeling walls, water stains, wall seepage, and grime. Wooden desks and chairs were aged with hand-carved scratches, scorching, and sandblasting. Metal window frames and filing cabinets got a dimensional rust-effect coating. Every aged surface was finished with a scratch-resistant clear protective coat, so the look wouldn't fade or chip during transport between venues or under heavy visitor contact.
#### Fear That Doesn't Depend on What You Can See
A 3D soundscape, delivered through multiple hidden directional speakers, placed radio static, distant footsteps, rain, a school bell, and a low-frequency heartbeat around the space to create psychological unease. A scent-engineering system used precision micro-vaporization diffusion to release damp aged wood, metallic blood, burning incense, and infirmary disinfectant into specific zones, triggering deep memory and fear directly.
Pneumatic and infrared-triggered mechanisms responded to visitors' footsteps along the route, setting off flashing lights, doors and windows slamming shut, and falling objects. NPC actors worked from concealed hiding points and ambush routes, coordinated with lighting and sound so every scare landed; the timing of every mechanism and every ambush was choreographed and tested repeatedly, until the sound of a scream became the most authentic feedback in the whole experience.
Classroom windows used real water-mist effects to simulate rain hitting glass, synced with cold air, scent, and sound. Select set walls and props were partially coated in fluorescent paint, switched under UV light to reveal hidden messages at specific story beats for a sudden jolt in the dark.
#### A Bright Green Exit Sign, at War With the Whole Mood
This was the real core challenge of the project. The game experience demanded extremely low light, a maze-like sense of enclosure, and large amounts of aged timber. Fire code demanded high-visibility exit signage, wide accessible circulation, and strictly fire-retardant materials. The two sets of requirements pulled in opposite directions, and we used four invisible-design techniques to hold onto the game's horror atmosphere in full while staying fully compliant.
The exit signage came first: a bright green EXIT sign left on at full brightness would have wrecked the low-light mood entirely. We built a smart evacuation-lighting system that, under normal conditions, used DMX central control to bring exit signage down to the lowest illuminance the code allows, or used shrouded fixtures casting only a faint downward glow. The moment a sensor triggered or someone pressed the emergency button, every hidden fixture and every bright green exit sign in the venue switched to 100% emergency brightness within 0.1 seconds, and every electronic hidden door unlocked at once.
Materials were the second conflict: the sheer volume of wood and vintage props failed Class-1 fire-retardancy requirements by default. Every wooden prop and finish material went through deep nano-fire-retardant impregnation, then got a Class-1 certified faux-flame-resistant composite coating on the surface, keeping the hand-aged texture intact while meeting code. Fabric props like curtains, student uniforms, and puppet-theater drapes went through colorless, odorless nano-fire-retardant impregnation and earned a national fire-retardant label.
Circulation was the third conflict: the main route kept a clear width of 1.2 to 1.5m or more to meet public-venue evacuation standards, while the walls used staggered placement, hanging debris, and low-light dark corners to create the visual sense of a corridor barely wide enough for one person. Hidden inside the long corridor and the midpoint of major sets were disguised secret doors, blended into the aged wall surface, functioning as staff-only passages under normal conditions and swinging open directly for rapid evacuation in an emergency.
Safety under low light was the fourth conflict: the entire zone kept a flat floor with no steps, any minor level changes were handled with gentle ramps, and baseboards carried an ultra-low-power LED strip at a wavelength that doesn't disrupt dark-adapted vision, preventing trips without breaking the darkness overhead.
#### Result
Four invisible-design solutions solved one contradiction: a frightening exhibition and a safe building didn't have to be a choice between the two.


---

## From Dragon to Beast

*Extinction and Radiation*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-dragon-to-beast.dc.html


**CLIENT:** National Museum of Natural Science · **LOCATION:** Taichung, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2013 · **CATEGORY:** Exhibition Design, Construction


#### 30 Meters of Fossil, 6 Meters of Wall
From Dragon to Beast was the largest, highest-specification international exhibition the National Museum of Natural Science had staged to date. Over a hundred rare fossils crossed the sea from the Gansu Geological Museum and the Hezheng Paleozoological Museum, including the largest and most completely preserved sauropod dinosaur ever discovered in Asia, the 30-meter-long Yongjing Titanosaur, alongside more than 140 significant pieces from the museum's own collection, many displayed outside mainland China for the first time. We took on the full design-build contract: display structures, custom cases, lighting and visual integration, flooring, and outdoor weatherproofing, against international-grade preservation standards, a tight schedule, and a highly complex mix of cross-disciplinary trades.
#### A Wall That Had to Stand on Its Own
The Dragon Hall was the centerpiece of the exhibition, an independent display wall standing 6 meters tall that had to carry the enormous suspended load of the giant dinosaur fossil and its heavy steel armature entirely on its own, without leaning on or damaging the existing building structure. Precise structural center-of-gravity calculations and load-distribution analysis led us to a self-supporting freestanding structural method: the wall itself became a complete structural system, holding up a 30-meter dinosaur without ever leaning on a single beam or column of the museum.
#### Sealed Once, No Second Chance
Under international museum preservation standards, once the fossils were positioned, the display case glass had to be sealed in a single pass, and from that moment until the end of the exhibition it couldn't be opened again. That meant every light fixture's angle, every color temperature, the microclimate humidity control inside the case, and the flatness of every finish surface had to be exactly right before the seal went on. There was no adjusting afterward; every parameter had to be the final answer on the first attempt.
#### Color as Geology
More than seven dedicated color schemes and lighting systems, one per display case, used color and optics as a metaphor for different geological eras, clearly separating fossil groups and evolutionary stages so visitors could sense they were walking through a journey spanning hundreds of millions of years just from the shifts in light and tone, without reading a single wall panel in full.
The floor got the same level of calculation: a high-strength raised timber flooring system with hidden LED light strips seamlessly embedded within it doubled as ambient exhibition lighting and safe wayfinding for large crowds, and the extended outdoor exhibition zone received additional high-standard moisture-proofing, UV resistance, and weatherproof coating to keep the wood flooring and display elements from warping or fading under prolonged sun and rain.
#### A Collapse Near the Finish Line
With installation nearly complete, an existing staircase, sealed off years earlier and unused for a long time, suddenly became structurally unstable, causing a localized floor collapse in the exhibition hall. We completed a safety-focused repair first, laying full carpet coverage over the area to keep the opening on schedule and circulation safe, and left the permanent structural repair for the museum to carry out through its standard procedures after the exhibition closed. The project was delivered with zero safety incidents and zero schedule delays, and the 30-meter dinosaur arrived in its hall exactly on time.


---

## Disaster Prevention Hall

*921 Earthquake Museum of Taiwan*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-engineering-construction.dc.html


**LOCATION:** Taichung, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2012 · **CATEGORY:** Construction


At 1:47 in the morning on September 21, 1999, Taiwan was hit by its largest earthquake in a century. Central Taiwan lost buildings across a wide swath of the region, and the disaster exposed how unprepared both rescue agencies and the public were.
Given Taiwan's geology and location, earthquakes, typhoons, and rockslides are bound to happen again, and preparation can't be treated as optional. The old saying holds: forewarned is forearmed, and prevention is worth more than any repair that comes after the fact. That is the founding purpose of the Disaster Prevention Hall: give visitors the knowledge to take refuge and respond, so a correct understanding of disaster prevention takes root before the next event arrives.
#### Site Conditions
The National Museum of Natural Science's 921 Earthquake Museum sits directly on the original site of the Chelungpu Fault. The building was designed and built around the ground-level offsets the fault's rupture had left behind, so its walls follow a curved line rather than a rectangular plan, and the floor slabs between zones differ in height by roughly 100 centimeters. Because that curvature and those level changes are part of the original architecture, construction couldn't correct them the way a normal building project would; every layout had to follow the existing curves and level shifts.
It got more complicated from there: the original exhibition design had been drawn up from architectural plans alone, without anyone surveying the site in person, so the curved walls and floor offsets on paper diverged noticeably from what was actually there. Setting-out baselines couldn't be taken from the drawings at all. The crew ended up templating each zone by hand on site, matching the real curvature zone by zone, which became the project's central technical problem.
#### Demolition and Measurement
Work started with tearing out the existing exhibits, display walls, partitions, and fixtures. As each section came down, the crew measured and logged the actual wall curvature and floor-level offsets zone by zone, building the reference data that later setting-out and fit-out work would depend on. Nothing about the curved lines or level changes at the core of the building's original design was allowed to be altered in the process.
#### Fit-Out
With the drawings unreliable and the curvature and offsets impossible to correct or hide, the crew templated every zone directly against the real geometry. New display walls and circulation fixtures were built on free-standing frames that didn't attach to the existing curved structure; each zone got its own vertical and horizontal reference lines set out from actual conditions, which let the new work hold proper precision and safety margins even inside a curved, uneven shell.
The roughly 100-centimeter floor offset was bridged with a combination of gentle ramps and stairs, keeping the level change itself visible as a piece of the building's original design rather than smoothing it away. The exhibition floor also carries a large run of angled laminated glass panels fixed with metal hardware, each pane individually adjusted to the real curvature of the walls and floor around it, which raised the bar on both construction precision and structural safety.
Flooring throughout was replaced entirely with seamless, through-body vinyl imported from Sweden, colored consistently from surface to core, resistant to wear, with no seams for dirt to collect in, built to take heavy sustained foot traffic while meeting the slip-resistance and cleaning standards a public educational venue needs.
#### Result
Once construction wrapped, the building, built originally around the fault's own ground-level offsets, held a full set of interactive disaster-prevention exhibits without losing its curved walls or level changes, letting the architecture's own design vocabulary sit in the same space as its educational content. The idea behind disaster-prevention education, preparing before disaster strikes, is now something visitors absorb directly through the building and the exhibits inside it, learning to respond to earthquakes, typhoons, and other hazards.


---

**CLIENT:** Fullchamp · **YEAR:** 2010 · **CATEGORY:** Graphic Design, Visual Design, Typography

## Wind, and Geothermal Energy Converge in a Single Pavilion

*TCCGE Green Energy Vision Pavilion*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-green-energy.dc.html


**CLIENT:** TCCGE · **LOCATION:** Changhua, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2022–Present · **CATEGORY:** Curatorial Project, Exhibition Design, Interior Design, Installation Art, Interactive Multimedia, Construction


Taiwan Cement Green Energy Corporation was set up in 2018 as a wholly owned subsidiary of the Taiwan Cement Group, tasked with building out the group's renewable energy business across solar, wind, and geothermal investment and development. By the end of 2019 the company had finished a 12.1MW solar array and a 7.2MW wind farm at Changbin. Around that same time, we were brought in to turn an adjacent space at the site into a public-facing exhibition hall, the Green Energy Vision Hall, built around the guiding statement "The future is worth it" and structured as a journey from interior to rooftop, from the mechanical to the organic.
#### Life and Cement, Grown Together
At the center of the exhibition sits a welcoming installation measuring 235 to 270 centimeters, in which plant life grows directly out of a cement structure, giving physical form to the idea of life and cement bound up together. It works as more than an entrance piece: it anchors the whole hall conceptually, framing the question of how a cement manufacturer builds, from its existing industrial base, toward a lasting commitment to environment and life.
The design proposal drew on Walter Benjamin's observation that in the face of life we hold no answers, only questions and the stories told while confronting them. That set the tone for the whole hall, which unfolds through narrative rather than lecturing visitors on energy facts, leaving room for people to explore at their own pace.
#### Entrance Sequence
The visitor route opens with a ceremonial corridor where rotating projected imagery asks who we are, where we come from, and where we are going. Taiwan Cement's shift from a traditional cement business toward renewable energy is framed here as an ongoing attempt to resolve problems between people, and between people and their environment. The sequence keeps its information density low on purpose, favoring atmosphere and emotional tone so visitors already feel connected to the subject before they reach the main exhibition space.
#### Finding Energy in the Environment
The core exhibition follows the logic of finding energy within the environment, unfolding zone by zone. The Energy Discovery Zone pairs a touch-interactive whiteboard with documentary footage tracing the Changbin plant's history from construction onward, using contextual graphics and text to build an understanding of how energy exists in nature.
The Real-Time Power and Renewable Energy Learning Zone links to the live energy monitoring center on the second floor and adds touch-based graphic interpretation, introducing renewable types such as biomass, hydro, tidal, and wave power alongside how each is developing in different countries. In the Household Electricity and Power Transmission Zone, sensor-activated lighting compares how much power different appliances draw, while the space explains AC/DC conversion and smart grid distribution; Kinect gesture detection combined with AR turns the abstract idea of electricity into something visitors can physically try.
The Solar, Wind, and Geothermal Zone lays out physical samples, cutaway models, and tablet-based games that explain how each of the three technologies generates power, with games supporting both solo play and two-player competition. A holographic interactive display cabinet lets visitors trigger three-dimensional animations at the press of a button, covering application scenarios for solar, wind, and geothermal energy and giving concrete shape to the idea of a green energy home.
The route closes in the Future Outlook Zone, built around seed banking and the carbon cycle, circling back to the exhibition's central line: "The future is worth it."
#### Onto the Roof
The narrative doesn't stop indoors. We also developed the rooftop into an outdoor viewing platform, giving visitors a vantage point over Taiwan Cement's working renewable energy site along with a dedicated photo spot.
#### Materials
Interior scenic surfaces rely heavily on board-formed concrete paired with woodwork, held up by a hot-dip galvanized C-channel steel structure that frames the three-dimensional feature walls. Zone D adds mirror-finished stainless steel spheres and blackened iron lettering to reinforce the forward-looking visual language. Multimedia work spans commercial touchscreens, a 270-degree infrared-touch holographic projection system, Kinect sensing devices, and custom interactive software, tying hardware, software, and spatial design into one connected system rather than a row of separate exhibits.
What started as a single installation of cement and living plants at the entrance carries through to a breathing green landscape on the roof, and across that arc, the Green Energy Vision Hall reads less as an exhibition and more as an enterprise renewing its dialogue with the environment it operates in.


---

## Enriching Hakka Settlements

*Camphor Industry Special Exhibition*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-hakka-culture.dc.html


**LOCATION:** Miaoli, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2012 · **CATEGORY:** Exhibition Design, Construction


#### Thirty Days, One Camphor Memory Hall
Thirty days. That's all the time there was between curatorial finalization and completion for the opening special exhibition of the Hakka Cultural Development Center's "Hidden Riches of the Hakka Villages" series, which took camphor as its subject. Taiwan once supplied 70 percent of the world's camphor; camphor, sugar, and tea were long called Taiwan's three treasures, and the Hakka villages of central and northern Taiwan formed the core production region.
The exhibition recreated the full chain of the industry, from harvesting and processing through to global trade, and extended into the transformation of Sanyi woodcarving, the Duck Box Treasure craft, and mask-based cultural creativity. We led the overall construction, turning academic research into something visitors could walk into, smell, and touch, on that thirty-day clock.
#### Why We Skipped Paint
Painting can only happen on site, and beyond slowing the schedule and generating dust that's hard to control, the smell would have competed with the camphor scent the whole exhibition was built around, leaving visitors smelling paint instead of camphor wood. So for the special-exhibit zone's partition system, we moved all the carpentry into factory-based modular prefabrication and left only assembly for the site, using laminate finishes across every surface instead of the traditional on-site spray-aging process. That took the most time-consuming, hardest-to-control, and most easily ruined step off site entirely.
The floor kept the museum's existing surface with a dark vinyl tile overlay defining the exhibition zone, and the accessible circulation width stayed at 120 centimeters or more throughout. At the entrance, a camphor sawdust scent basin paired with a low-speed, silent fan diffuser sends the camphor's volatile scent through the entire hall rather than just the doorway, so visitors are inside the smell before they've read a single panel.
#### Handling What a Century Left Behind
The artifact cases are museum-grade: solid-wood mortise-and-tenon bases with low-iron, low-reflection glass at over 91 percent transmittance, so glare doesn't get in the way of reading the objects. Passive humidity-control boxes inside manage the microclimate for organic artifacts like the Japanese-colonial-era ledgers and camphor crystals, materials that are damaged by both damp and dryness and need the humidity to settle on its own rather than being forced by outside control.
The exhibition shows real camphor wood at different processing stages, from raw cut blocks to the crushed feedstock used just before distillation, alongside actual Sanyi camphor-wood carvings and other craft pieces, tracing the material's path from raw wood to industrial technique to craft. Photographic panels lay out the full camphor-shed and distillation process, and a 1:10 scale model of a camphor-shed work scene compresses the division of labor across logging, gathering, and distillation into something visitors can take in at a glance.
#### Light, Held to a Standard
The zone runs on 3000K warm-white lighting, with track lights and 15-degree narrow-beam spotlights on the artifacts, illuminance held between 50 and 150 lux, the fixed range for paper-artifact preservation with no margin either way.
The camphor-tree feature zone is built from real camphor material sourced from a nearby camphor factory, showing the material from whole timber down to crushed feedstock, lit with wall-wash fixtures to create a dappled forest-light effect that makes the zone both a visual centerpiece and a working teaching aid on the processing chain. The timeline wall and the "Hakka Settlements and Camphor-Producing Regions" map use UV direct printing with an anti-glare film, and the interpretive panels use acid-free mounting with dimensional cut lettering, so nothing warps or discolors over a long run.
The whole schedule was built around the center's opening date, with night-shift work and zone-by-zone enclosed construction; display cases were pre-assembled at the factory and only brought in for final installation, which kept dust from reaching the museum's other permanent exhibits. A full round of illuminance, temperature-and-humidity, and emergency-evacuation testing was completed before the doors opened. Thirty days, and a museum-grade exhibition holding artifact preservation, industrial storytelling, and immersive experience together, all under a deadline that had already been announced to the public.


---

## Opening Day, and Not One of the 93 Fossils Could Be Late

*Jehol Biota*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-jehol-biota.dc.html


**CLIENT:** National Museum of Natural Science · **LOCATION:** Taichung, Taiwan · **YEAR:** 2019–2020 · **AREA:** 991.737㎡ · **CATEGORY:** Construction


991.737 square meters, 93 fossil specimens, and an opening date that had already been announced to the public and international partners before the fit-out even started. That was the frame for the Jehol Biota Special Exhibition at the National Museum of Natural Science, which brought rare fossils from western Liaoning, China, dating back roughly 125 million years to the early Cretaceous, jointly curated with the NMNS Education Foundation and the Beijing Museum of Natural History. It marked the formal Taiwan debut of one of the twentieth century's most significant paleontological discoveries.
The exhibition was organized into three zones, "Entering the Jehol Biota," "Encountering the Jehol Biota," and "Witnessing the Evidence of Flight," and the 93 specimens included Scansoriopteryx and Microraptor gui. Among the highlights: China's first mummified Psittacosaurus fossil with clearly preserved skin impressions, the exhibition's largest specimen in a Jinzhousaurus fossil, and a Microraptor gui specimen with its feather melanin granules fully intact, evidence that matters directly to the study of how dinosaurs evolved into birds.
We served as the construction contractor, converting the museum's existing hall into a professional display environment that met international academic-collaboration standards and fossil-preservation requirements.
#### What the Fit-Out Had to Carry
These were precious fossil artifacts on international loan, so the venue had to meet the baseline temperature, humidity, seismic, and dust-control conditions required for museum-grade artifact display, keeping the loaned material safe and intact for the run of the show. The fit-out was also built zone by zone to match the exhibition's entering-encountering-witnessing narrative structure, so visitors would work through the science of the Jehol Biota step by step. Most specimens needed dedicated display cases and interpretive graphic systems, and every decision had to hold artifact-preservation standards and visual presentation in balance, since neither one could be allowed to compromise the other.
#### Working Backward From a Fixed Date
This was an international academic collaboration, and the opening date had already been made public, which left no room to slip. We worked backward from that fixed point: how long installation would take, how long the fossil specimens would need to arrive, how long positioning the display cases would take, compressing the entire fit-out into that window while still leaving enough buffer to guarantee the show would open on time regardless of what went wrong along the way. All 93 fossils, some of them hundreds of millions of years old, showed up exactly on schedule in their new home in Taiwan.

## La Fortuna Bordada

Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-la-fortuna-bordada.dc.html


**LOCATION:** Madrid, Spain · **YEAR:** 2017 · **CATEGORY:** Exhibition Design, Interior Design, Graphic Design, Visual Design, Logo Design


#### Never Once on Site
"La Fortuna Bordada: Taiwanese Embroidery from the Collection of the National Museum of History" opened at Spain's Museo Nacional de Artes Decorativas, the first time Taiwanese embroidery craft has been shown in full within Spain's national museum system, made possible after two years of work by Taiwan's Representative Office in Spain. The National Museum of History holds nearly a thousand pieces of Taiwanese clothing and everyday embroidery dating from the latter half of the nineteenth century onward, and this show selected 74 groups from that collection, presented under two themes: everyday dress and accessories, and officials' rank badges. We handled the spatial planning and exhibition construction design for the show. Across the entire project, though, we never had a single person on the ground in Madrid.
#### Design in Taiwan, Delivered as Drawings
With the artifacts needing international shipping and the venue on the other side of the world, we worked in a design-in-Taiwan, deliver-by-drawings model. The full spatial plan and every piece of display-fixture design was completed on the Taiwan side, then converted into a complete set of construction drawings and handed to a local Spanish contractor to build and install.
There was no way to stand on site and supervise, and no way to go back the next day and fix something that didn't work, so the drawings had to spell out every detail on their own. They were the only language we had to communicate with the construction team in Spain.
#### What the Display Stands Had to Account For
Embroidered artifacts are fragile, sensitive to light damage, and can't hold up under long-term hanging tension, so we designed dedicated case structures and a garment-suspension system around those limits. Small three-dimensional accessories like purses, embroidered shoes, and children's caps each have their own shape, so we designed acrylic display stands individually for each category, custom-fitting the support structure to the contour of every piece. All of that had to be resolved completely at the design stage, since once the pieces reached Spain there was no room left to adjust anything.
The key visuals and printed graphics translated the auspicious symbolism carried by the flowers, fruit, birds, and animals in the embroidery patterns into a visual storytelling system Western audiences could read intuitively, so cultural distance never got in the way of understanding.
This is one of the few overseas museum projects we've delivered entirely through drawings. We were never on site, and yet through a single complete set of construction documents, all 74 groups of embroidered artifacts were hung and cased in Madrid with every dimension in place.


---

## Universe

*500 Pieces of LED Kinetic Light*


Source: https://www.letsuan.com/project-led-kinetic.dc.html


**CLIENT:** Grandview Mall Science Museum · **LOCATION:** Canton, China · **YEAR:** 2024 · **CATEGORY:** Exhibition Design, Installation Art, Interactive Multimedia, Construction


500 kinetic LED fixtures, one winch system per fixture, and a single piece of control software tying it all together, that's the mechanical core of "Cosmos," the dynamic lighting installation we designed for the Science Museum at Guangzhou's Grandview Mall. It works double duty as functional illumination and as the space's visual focal point, and it's paired with music and narration to guide visitors toward an intuitive understanding of astronomical knowledge. We handled the design planning for the lighting installation on this project.
#### Concept
The installation takes the vastness of the cosmos as its central image. The 500-fixture array translates astronomical phenomena into a visualized language of light and shadow, and inside a setting woven from sound and light, visitors pick up on the movement of celestial bodies and the abstract scale of the universe without needing it explained to them.
#### Technical Planning
Each fixture's vertical position is controlled by its own winch, while LED RGB modules handle color and brightness, both folded into the same specialized control software. During design, we worked out the synchronization logic between the winches' motion paths and the lighting's color transitions, so the array could build varied, layered forms and light effects under precise choreography rather than just moving up and down, which is what gives the piece its combination of fine detail and dynamic tension.
